chapter_theme: Portraits of the noble (மேன்மக்கள்): they cannot bear a stain, aim high whatever the outcome, stay within bounds in want, keep their speech clean under abuse and welcome those who come to ask. Wealth draws the base, but meeting the well-born is the real treasure.
structure_note: Most quatrains pair a natural image (moon, arrow, worn path, sugar-cane, treasure cave) with a trait of the noble. Mudaliar's note on 151 reads மேன்மக்கள் as the high-born, while the verses themselves mostly describe conduct.

151.reading: The noble resemble the moon that spreads its light across the sky, except that the moon carries its spot while the noble, if one stain falls on them, pine away and waste.
151.nuance: The comparison turns into a contrast: the moon is the lesser because it puts up with its blemish. Sensitivity to stain is made the mark of superiority.

positions.position: Because the moon is specified as the moon in the wide sky, the 'noble' of the chapter title are to be taken as the high-born.
positions.quote: 'மேன்மக்கள்' உயர் குடிப் பிறப்புடையார் என்பது குறிப்பிற் கொள்க

152.reading: Whether the aim succeeds or not, the worthy plan only what carries no blame: is the arrow that missed a lion worse than the one that tore open a jackal's breast?
152.nuance: Two ideas sit together: the aim must be blameless, and it must be high. A noble failure outranks a mean success.

153.reading: Though poverty leaves them all sinew, the worthy do not cross the bounds into wrongdoing; binding the mind with understanding and resolve, they do what ought to be done as far as their means allow.
153.nuance: The last phrase sets a measure: duty is scaled to what one has, not abandoned. 185 ends with the same words, செய்வர் செயற்பாலவை.

154.reading: If the worthy see someone just once on the road, they bind that person to them as if in a friendship of long standing, just as a few days' treading makes a path even over rock.
154.nuance: The image cuts two ways: a path on rock needs repeated treading, yet the worthy form the bond at one meeting. Pope adds that those so bound are themselves worthy; the Tamil does not say so.

155.reading: When an unlearned man who knows neither grammar nor meaning speaks in an empty gathering, the good listen out of kindly regard, though it pains them, to spare him shame before many.
155.nuance: Mudaliar glosses கண்ணோடி as தாட்சிண்யம், courteous indulgence. The good endure bad speech not for its sake but for the speaker's face.

156.reading: Sugar-cane bitten, crushed at the joints and pounded for its juice is still sweet; so the well-born, even when abused so as to wound, do not lose themselves and speak in kind.
156.nuance: Shanmuganar reads the close as positive, that they keep speaking sweetly; the Tamil says only that they do not speak as people undone.

157.reading: Those of faultless vision do not steal, do not drink, shun what is forbidden, do not scorn others, and never lie even by a slip; and if they decline in fortune, they do not grieve.
157.nuance: The list of abstentions ends in an inner state: equanimity in decline is presented as the fruit of clean conduct.

158.reading: One who is deaf to others' secrets, blind to a neighbour's wife and dumb in evil backbiting, knowing what is fitting, needs no teaching of virtue at all.
158.nuance: Mudaliar reads 'if he stands so' as stressing how rare this is. Virtue here is a matter of restraint of the senses, not of instruction.

159.reading: Those without good character scorn a frequent visitor, thinking he wants something from them; the excellent, thinking it good even if he asks, honour him every time they see him.

160.reading: The base settle on the rich as their one hope and live by trailing after them; yet meeting people of good family is like coming upon a treasure cave.
160.nuance: The contrast is between attaching oneself to money and to lineage. The verse prizes good birth as company; it does not say what the treasure consists of.

links.note: Both use the spot on the moon. In 957 the fault of the well-born shows as plainly as the moon's spot; in 151 the noble differ from the moon in being unable to live with the spot at all.
Both make honour a matter of life and death: in 969 the honourable give up life like the yak that loses its hair, and in 151 the noble waste away at a single stain.
Aim high regardless of outcome: 596 says a lofty aim, even if thwarted, keeps its worth, and 152 says the arrow that misses a lion beats the one that kills a jackal.
Want does not license wrongdoing. 656 holds even if one's mother starves; 153 holds even when one's own body is reduced to sinew.
785 says long acquaintance is not needed for friendship, only shared feeling; 154 shows the worthy treating a single meeting as an old bond.

791 warns that nothing ruins like befriending without inquiry, since the true friend cannot later withdraw. 154 praises binding someone seen once as if an old friend. The tension holds if 154 means any passer-by; Pope's parenthetical '(worthy) men' softens it, but the Tamil has no such qualifier.
153 calls bearing with fools the strength of strengths; 155 shows that strength as patient listening to an ignorant speaker so as not to shame him.
403 puts the burden on the unlearned: they are good if they stay silent before the learned. 155 takes the case where they do not, and puts the burden on the learned to endure it kindly.
Both use crushed sugar-cane, to opposite ends. In 1078 the base are like cane, giving only when crushed; in 156 the well-born are like cane, still sweet however crushed.
159 makes bearing harsh words from the insolent as pure as renunciation; 156 makes it the mark of good birth.
Both say the virtuous cannot speak evil even by a slip: வழுக்கியும் in 139, தள்ளியும் in 157.
148 calls not looking at another's wife both virtue and complete conduct; 158 makes that blindness one of three abstentions that leave nothing more to teach.

Both give one abstention near-sufficient moral weight: 181 says it is good to be called one who does not backbite even if one does wrong, and 158 counts silence in backbiting among the restraints that make virtue-teaching unnecessary.
224 admits that being asked is painful until one sees the asker's glad face; 159 describes the excellent as treating the prospect of being asked as good from the outset.
1057 is the asker's side: the heart rejoices at givers who do not scorn. 159 is the giver's side: the excellent honour those who may ask instead of scorning them.
443 calls winning the great as one's own the rarest of all things; 160 calls meeting the well-born a treasure cave, against the base who chase the rich.

source_issues: 151: Pope's text is garbled ('while the truly worthy endure it. not;'); the sense is that the worthy do not endure a stain.
152: Tamil has a corrupted character in நா஢மா, which Mudaliar's gloss shows is நரிமா.
157: Tamil reads கடிந்தெரிணஇ, apparently a corruption of கடிந்தொரீஇ, as Mudaliar's gloss 'கடிவ கடிந்து ஒரீஇ' shows.
159: Tamil reads விமுமியோர், a typo for விழுமியோர் (Mudaliar's gloss has விழுமியோர்).
